idiom_name: explicit init() called from main + __attribute__((constructor)) pre-allocation
implementation_notes: C has no runtime bootstrap and no module system, so eager acquisition is code you write: a service-init function called from main() (portable, testable, ordering under your control) that pre-opens descriptors, pre-spawns threads and pre-allocates buffers, or a function marked __attribute__((constructor)), which GCC documents as running before main() - with the caveat that its order relative to other static initialisation is unspecified and that priorities 0-100 are reserved for the compiler and runtime. Keep cross-resource ordering in the explicit init() path and use the attribute only for self-contained, order-independent setup. Where the acquisition can also be entered from another thread, pthread_once is defined to run the init routine exactly once, which is the standard way to make the start-up step idempotent.
pitfalls: The constructor attribute is a GNU extension whose ordering against other static initialisation is unspecified, so a constructor that depends on another module's state is a start-up bug waiting for a link-order change.
There are no exceptions to carry an acquisition failure, so an unchecked allocation or pool-open result turns into a null dereference at first use instead of a diagnosable boot failure.
Descriptors, threads and pools acquired before fork() are inherited by every child, so a pre-fork eager setup appears shared - re-open per child or acquire after the fork.
